messages.subject: Occu function
parts:
Hi,

I am using the occu function to fit models of occupancy/detection considering different variables.

One of the models includes the variable "Elevation" (in m) which I previously standardised (i.e. mean 0 and SD 1) using the function decostand. However, when I look at the newly created model I get a Warning message that I don't fully understand.I am not sure what it means by: "Try providing starting values or increasing maxit control argment".

> o3_4<-occu(~1~Elevation,data)

> o3_4


Call:

occu(formula = ~1 ~ Elevation, data = elbaOo4)

Occupancy:

            Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)

(Intercept)     57.9  63.4 0.913   0.361

Elevation       92.5 101.4 0.912   0.362

Detection:

 Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)

    -1.56 0.204 -7.63 2.28e-14

AIC: 160.6721 

Warning message:

In (new("standardGeneric", .Data = function (object)  :

  Model did not converge. Try providing starting values or increasing maxit control argment.


Any ideas on what I should do next? Thank you very much for your help.

Ettore

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Occu function
parts:
Thanks, Ettore.

One comment: You have a very small data set with only 11 sites, so probably should not add more than a single site covariate into the occupancy model. But this does not necessary explain your problem.

Perhaps it's a problem of complete separation: that's when in a logistic regression (and the occupancy part of the model is one) some value of a covariate completely separates all 0s and all 1s in the response, then usual maximum likelihood will get infinity.

I think I would explore your data set with a simple logistic regression first: i.e., model the indicator for whether the beast is ever detected over the 21 surveys (= 1) or not (=0). You have 11 values of the response then. That will emphasize to you the sparsity of your data set, but also perhaps lets you better diagnose causes for your problem.

Assuming that the estimates in your model fit are not totally of the mark, I see that p is estimated at plogis(-1.56) = 0.1736466. So, this means that the combined detection probability in your study is 1 - (1-0.1736466)^21 = 0.98. So you won't risk much when you ignore imperfect detection in this case perhaps.

Best regards  -- Marc
